title: Low midpoint tails had more next-day persistence at San Francisco and Seattle in retained 1996-2024 records
abstract: We tested whether high and low daily water-level midpoint anomalies have equal next-day tail persistence at six US gauges. We used 61,242 station-days from fixed NOAA CO-OPS snapshots in retained 1996-2024 months. Each midpoint is the mean of hourly daily maximum and minimum, minus monthly mean sea level. Site and calendar-month thresholds select the lowest and highest 5% of values. The high-tail minus low-tail next-day probability was -10.00 percentage points at San Francisco and -29.37 points at Seattle. Intervals adjusted for six site comparisons were -15.25 to -1.23 and -32.23 to -18.94 points. The other four adjusted site intervals included zero. The equal-site mean was -4.65 points, with a 95% three-year block interval of -6.29 to -1.77 points after threshold refitting. Omitting Seattle changed the mean to +0.29 points. A post hoc fixed lunar filter reduced, but did not remove, the descriptive Seattle contrast. The midpoint is not measured surge. Selected sites, daily sampling, tide structure, missing data, and bootstrap assumptions limit inference. No flood duration, recovery, trend, or physical cause is established. The package gives source hashes, daily evidence, all resampling weights and estimates, code, a figure, and independent audits.

display.caption: High- and low-tail next-day probabilities and high minus low differences at six selected US gauges in retained 1996-2024 records. Site intervals use a six-site Bonferroni adjustment. Monthly mean removal and daily extrema do not isolate storm surge.
